title: DeepSeek separates step limits from whole-answer budgets
dek: DeepSeek’s expanded app APIs put search on the server. A familiar output limit applies to each inference step, not the entire round.
lede: DeepSeek released its full suite of application APIs on November 13, bringing more of its chat application into developer integrations. The release makes a budgeting distinction important: one visible answer can contain several server-managed inference steps.

facts.label: Thinking search
facts.value: Up to about 20 tool calls before answering

body.heading: What moved into the service?
body.text: DeepSeek’s release combines built-in conversation features with standalone tools. The announcement covers search, files, links, safety and voice, alongside an open-source chat demonstration. For developers, the relevant change is where orchestration happens. A request can ask the service to assemble context and perform searches, instead of making the application run every intermediate action. The release is therefore useful context for examining what a request limit actually controls. A shared endpoint format does not make all parameter meanings interchangeable.

body.heading: Which limit applies to a step?
body.text: The chatbot guide says max_tokens, called max_output_tokens in Responses, limits each inference step within a round. It does not cap the round’s combined output. The guide also lists parameters the service ignores when web tools, high-level safety checking or title generation activate this mode. These include max_tool_calls in Responses. A setting present in a client library can therefore remain in the request without controlling the operation its name suggests. The integration boundary includes both accepted fields and their documented effect.

body.heading: How does that change a budget calculation?
body.text: Consider an illustrative request with a limit of 1,000 output tokens per step. If three steps each produce 800 tokens, their combined output is 2,400 tokens. Each step remains below 1,000. These numbers describe arithmetic, not a measured DeepSeek run or a prediction of its bills. The distinction matters for a product that promises a fixed allowance per answer: a step-sized limit and an answer-sized allowance measure different units. Input processing and tool use introduce additional accounting categories beyond the example’s output total.

body.heading: What does a search round contain?
body.text: DeepSeek’s Web Tools guide describes deep thinking search as a sequence of searches, page openings and text lookups. It gives an approximate ceiling of twenty tool calls before an answer. A tool call and an inference step are different events, so multiplying that figure by an output limit would not establish a precise round budget. The model chooses whether to search. Direct Search and Fetch endpoints provide a separate route when an application wants to issue those operations itself.

body.heading: When is a returned answer finished?
body.text: The Responses reference distinguishes completed, incomplete and failed states. Its streaming protocol ends with an event identifying one of those outcomes. An application can receive useful-looking text before reaching that terminal state. The reference also defines usage fields and error details, which separate content from accounting and completion information. In practical terms, displaying a partial answer, accepting a finished answer and recording resource consumption are three separate application decisions. A visible paragraph alone cannot settle all three.

body.heading: Where does responsibility remain?
body.text: Server-managed execution reduces the amount of orchestration an application implements, while leaving its product-level acceptance rules intact. An application’s allowance, timeout policy and definition of a complete answer still need explicit meanings. For the hypothetical budget above, a per-step guard prevents an oversized individual step; a whole-answer ledger answers a different question. The new suite makes that separation more relevant because several capabilities now sit behind a single conversation request. The central integration task is matching each product promise to the boundary that actually enforces it.

buildersNote: Run 10 representative requests with web tools enabled. Record terminal status, total reported token usage and tool counts separately; compare those records with your per-answer allowance before setting a customer quota.

claims.text: DeepSeek documents the output limit as per inference step, not per complete round.
Deep thinking search makes up to about 20 tool calls before answering, according to the guide.
A particular application will remain below its monetary budget using these settings alone.

social.hook: One answer can contain several separately limited steps.
social.voiceover: [measured] One answer can contain several separately limited steps. DeepSeek brought its app tools to developers. Thinking search can make about twenty tool calls. A step limit is not an answer budget.
social.short: DeepSeek opened its app tools through three API formats. Its output limit applies per inference step, not per complete answer. A whole-answer budget needs separate accounting.
social.long:
DeepSeek’s new app APIs move search orchestration onto the service. The November 13 release lets developers combine more conversation capabilities without running every intermediate action themselves.

The useful distinction is between a request field and a product promise. A per-step limit does not establish a fixed allowance for a complete answer. We would keep completion status and resource accounting separate from the text shown to a user. Actual spending still depends on the workload.
social.take: We favor measuring complete answers before promising a fixed allowance. Familiar parameter names are a poor substitute for checking which boundary they control.
keyFacts: 3 API formats support the chat features
